claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the selected equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
The quaternary and ternary subsets can be produced by removing one or two elements, such as Cr and/or Mn, from the quinary alloy while retaining equiatomic proportions.
Interactions among all five elements produce SRO and local-solute-clustering patterns distinct from those in the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has more robust SRO than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
SRO and local solute clusters create localized lattice distortions.
SRO and local solute clusters act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The quinary alloy's SRO increases dislocation pinning relative to the reduced subsets.
The distinct chemical ordering in the quinary alloy modifies stacking-fault energy relative to the reduced subsets.
The distinct chemical ordering in the quinary alloy disrupts slip transfer relative to the reduced subsets.
Reduced elemental complexity produces diminished or differently organized SRO in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Differences in SRO cause differences in yield strength and strain-hardening behavior among the alloys.
Under identical test conditions, the quinary alloy will have higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Under identical test conditions, the quinary alloy will exhibit greater strain hardening than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will exhibit localized dislocation pinning correlated with robust SRO features.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit more homogeneous dislocation distributions and lower mechanical resistance than the quinary alloy.
The SRO-mediated differences will produce altered failure modes in the quinary alloy relative to the reduced subsets.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature deformation of single-phase FCC alloys with matched processing histories and controlled strain rates.
APT, scattering, and in-situ deformation measurements can be combined to test correlations among SRO, stacking-fault energy, and dislocation behavior.
